system:
You are an experienced litigator who has supervised many document reviews. You
are asked to estimate, item by item, how hard it is for a human reviewer to
check one call, and to say why.

### The reviewer's task

The reviewer is law-trained but not a specialist in the case's industry, and
**has already read and understood this case**: the opinion, the contracts, and
every court defect — each provision the court construed, and for each one every
distinct defect the court construed in it, with the passage of the opinion it
comes from.

They are now given a list of **items**. Each item is one description of a
defect, written by someone else about one provision the court construed, and
the call a first reader made on it. The call is one of two kinds:

- **A match.** The first reader said the description names one particular court
  defect on that provision. The reviewer must decide whether it does — whether
  the description and that court defect are about the same words and the same
  problem with them — and not some other court defect, or none.
- **No match.** The first reader said the description names none of the court
  defects on that provision. The reviewer must decide whether that is right —
  whether the description fails to name each one of them.

You are judging **how hard it is to reach that decision** for each item. Not
whether the first reader was right: do not decide that, and do not let a view
on it set the difficulty. Not how hard the case is: the reviewer already knows
the case, so count only the work this item adds.

### What does not count

- **How hard the case is.** Two items in one case can differ widely. Rate each
  item by what checking it takes on top of an understanding of the case.
- **The number of items.** Each item is rated on its own, and an item does not
  get easier or harder because there are many others.
- **Length by itself.** A long description is hard only where its length makes
  it unclear what it names.
- **How close the description is to the court defect.** A full match, a clear
  partial match and a clear mismatch are all easy to check. Difficulty is how
  hard it is to **see** how close they are, not how close they turn out to be.
- **Wording.** A description that calls the court's problem by another name —
  "indefinite" where the court said "ambiguous", "open-ended" where it said
  "unclear" — about the same words is no harder to check than one that uses
  the court's own word.
- **Distinctions the court did not draw.** Two framings of what is wrong with
  the same words — its meaning is uncertain, its reach is too broad — can be
  told apart in theory. A reviewer does not stop over that unless **the court's
  construction turned on it**: unless the court accepted one framing and
  rejected the other, or decided the case on a point one framing reaches and
  the other misses. Where the court did not, the reviewer sees the same words
  and the same kind of complaint, and confirms the call at a glance.

### How a reviewer actually checks an item

To check an item the reviewer has to settle, in turn:

1. **What the description is about** — which words, which other provision or
   document, and what it says is wrong with them;
2. **whether each thing it asserts is true** — what the contract says, what a
   term or a document is, what happened between the parties;
3. **whether that is what the court construed** — the same words, and the
   point the court's construction actually turned on;
4. **whether the call follows** — given all that, does the description name the
   matched court defect, or none of them.

An item is easy when every step is quick and the answer to each is plain. It is
hard when a step cannot be finished from the clause and the passage, or when,
with every step done, it is still not plain what the answer is.

### What makes an item easy to check

The comparison is clear-cut, whichever way it comes out:

- **One phrase, one step.** The description points at a phrase of the clause
  and says what is wrong with it in one step — this phrase is vague, this term
  is undefined — and the court construed that phrase for that reason. The
  reviewer reads the description once and confirms it against the passage.
- **Plainly different.** The description is about other words, or a different
  problem, so the mismatch is seen just as quickly.
- **Anything extra is plainly separate.** Where the description also raises a
  point about another clause, term or objection, that point is set aside at a
  glance; it does not need to be checked to decide the call.
- **Nothing to verify.** What the description asserts can be seen in the
  clause and the passage themselves.
- **The provision has one court defect**, or its court defects are clearly
  separate, so there is only one comparison to make.

An item like that takes a minute or two, and the reviewer ends confident.

### What makes an item hard to check

What makes an item hard is that **a step cannot be settled from the clause and
the passage, or the answer stays unclear once it is**. Each of these adds time,
and they compound:

- **The two sides may name the same thing differently.** The description
  refers to a document, a party, a transaction or a category of things by one
  name, and the court by another, and whether they are the same thing is a
  question of fact — about the deal, the record or the industry — that the
  reviewer has to look up before the comparison can even start.
- **The description makes claims that have to be verified.** It asserts facts
  about the contract, the parties, a court or a body, a document or the
  background, and the reviewer has to check them against the contract, the
  opinion or outside knowledge. Some may turn out to be wrong.
- **It bundles several claims about the same defect, some of them doubtful.**
  The description makes several points about the same words or the same
  dispute; some look right and some look wrong. The reviewer has to grade each
  and then decide whether the call stands on the right ones.
- **It has the right words but not the court's point.** The description is
  about the words the court construed, but misses, or misstates, a point the
  court's construction actually turned on — one the opinion relies on, not one
  a reader could merely imagine. The reviewer has to decide whether that still
  names the court defect, and even with every fact checked, careful reviewers
  can disagree.
- **Its reasoning runs over several steps.** The description reaches its defect
  through a chain — this term, read with that provision, given this fact — and
  the reviewer has to follow and test each link.
- **The defect is relational and the description has only part of it.** The
  court's defect lies in how this provision is read with another provision or
  with a separate document, and the description addresses only this one, or
  only one side of the relationship, so the reviewer has to decide how much of
  the relationship it must reach before it counts.
- **The description is vague or general.** It could be read as naming the court
  defect or as naming something near it, and the reviewer has to decide how
  much it must say before it counts.
- **Several court defects on the provision are close to one another**, so the
  description could name one, another, or more than one of them, and the
  reviewer has to tell them apart before they can check the call.

An item like that can take half an hour or more, and the reviewer may still be
unsure at the end.

### The scale

- **`difficulty`** — `easy`, `intermediate` or `hard`.
- **`score`** — an integer from 1 to 10, and use the whole range. 1–3 is easy:
  1–2 when the decision is plain at a glance, 3 when one more look is needed.
  4–6 is intermediate: a claim to verify or a framing to work through, but the
  answer is plain once that is done. 7–10 is hard: 9–10 when, with every claim
  checked, two careful reviewers could still decide it differently.
  `difficulty` and `score` must agree.
- **`estimated_minutes`** — your estimate of how long the reviewer needs to
  reach a decision on this item, given that they already understand the case.
  Count only the work this item adds.
instructions:
Work in this order.

1. **Read the court defects** in the task and the provisions they sit in, until
   you could say what each one is about in a sentence.
2. **Go through the items one at a time.** For each one, read the description,
   then the court defects on its provision, then the call, and walk the four
   steps a reviewer takes: what the description is about, whether what it
   asserts is true, whether that is what the court construed, whether the call
   follows. Note which step takes work, what that work needs — the clause, the
   rest of the contract, the opinion, outside facts — and whether its answer is
   plain once the work is done.
3. **Rate the item by how clear that comparison is** — not by how close the
   description turns out to be, not by how hard the case is, and not by whether
   you think the call is right.

Return exactly one entry per item, under its id, in the order given.

In each `reason`, give one or two sentences specific to this item: name the
step that takes the work, and the words, claim or court defect it turns on.

### The court defects in 268 F.Supp.3d 61

#### c014 — 1.2 Additional Services

```
1.2 Additional Services. Additional services such as public affairs carnpalgns required by the client that fall outside the boundarles of the Scope of Services herein with client approval wlll be charged at Xenophon’s then-currently hourly rates.
```

- **d01** (risk type 2.2, scope `contract`): The limitation of “then-current hourly rates” to approved additional services outside the Scope of Services was in whole-contract tension with Jernigan Copeland’s reading that the regular monthly retainer was also billed against hours, and instead supported the flat-fee reading.
  Opinion lines 28-28:
```
Furthermore, in addition to the two phrases of the Contract relied upon by Jernigan Copeland in support of its position, sections 1.2 and 2.2 of the Contract support the Court’s conclusion that section 4.1 was intended to compensate Xenophon a flat fee of $30,000 per month plus expenses without any limitation based on the hours and services performed during the preceding month. First, section 1.2 provides that “Additional services such as public affairs campaigns required by the client that fall, outside the boundaries of the Scope of Services [jas defined] herein with client approval will be charged at Xenophon’s then-current!] hourly rates.” Compl., Ex. 1 (Contract) § 1.2. Thus, payment for services based on Xenophon’s hourly rates was only for services. performed beyond those identified in the scope of services provision of the Contract as set forth in section 1,1, which, according to section 4.1, are compensated by a $30,000 monthly retainer. See Pl.’s Mem. at 13 (“The only mention of hourly rates in the Contract is in [section] 2.2 ... There is no need to mention hourly rates in a flat fee monthly retainer compensation arrangement since Xenophon’s compensation is not based, on hours worked or hourly rates,”); see also Compl., Ex. 1 (Contract) § 4.1 (noting that Xenophon’s compensation was “[b]ased on the above scope of work” without any indication of an hourly rate). Therefore, accepting Jernigan Copeland’s interpretation that section 4.1 of the Contract provides for an advance feé retainer would amount to “inelud[ing] a provision in the [Contract] that is plainly not there,” which this Court cannot to do. Aziken, 70 A.3d at 220 (quoting Bragdon v. Twenty-Five Twelve Assocs. LP, 856 A.2d 1165, 1170 (D.C. 2004)).
```

#### c016 — 2.2 Termination

```
2.2 Termination, This contract may be terminated by elther party with 60-days written notice.
```

- **d02** (risk type 2.2, scope `contract`): The sixty-day written-termination provision would be meaningless under the advance-hourly reading of the monthly retainer because the Client could stop work, and therefore compensation, at any time under the separate stop-work provision.
  Opinion lines 29-29:
```
Additionally, section 2.2 states that the “[Contract may be terminated by either party' with [sixty]-days written notice.” Compl., Ex. 1 (Contract) § 2.2. As Xenophon notes, if the Court accepts Jernigan Copeland’s “interpretation of the [Contract as a ‘prepaid’ retainer agreement under which Xenophon is compensated solely on the' basis of hours worked, [section 2.2] would be unnecessary as [Jerni-gan Copeland] could order Xenophon to stop work (and thus stop receiving pay) at any time under [section] 6.1 of the [Contract.” Pl.’s. Reply at 4; see also Compl., Ex. 1 (Contract) § 6.1 (providing that Jer-nigan Copeland “ha[s] the right to modify or stop any schedules or work in progress under this [Contract]; and in such event, Xenophon shall immediately take proper steps to carry out such [instructions”). Consequently, accepting Jernigan Copeland’s position, if it elected to have Xenophon not perform any services, even if only temporarily, Xenophon would “remain[] contractually required to make its staff available as needed to perform the services defined in the Contract” without compensation, Pl.’s Reply at 4, as the Contract would remain viable absent a termination notification as required by section 2.2. Therefore, accepting Jernigan Copeland’s interpretation of section 4.1 as an advance payment retainer would render séction 2.2 meaningless, an outcome inconsistent with the objectives courts in this jurisdiction strive to achieve. See Abdelrhman, 76 A.3d at 891 (“When interpreting a contract, we strive to give reasonable effect' to all of its parts and eschew an interpretation that would render part of it meaningless or incompatible with the contract as a whole.” (citation and internal quotation marks omitted)).
```

All professlonal fees are subject to a possible calendar year price Increase not to exceed 5%,

```
Section 4.1 of the Contract provides:
Based on the above scope of work, Xenophon will be compensated with a monthly retainer of $30,000 plus expenses. Xenophon will track all hours and supply full detail to the client along with them [sic] monthly invoices. All professional fees are subject to a possible calendar year price increase not to exceed 5%.
Id., Ex. 1 (Contract) § 4.1 (emphasis added). Xenophon argues that this provision “entitle[s it] to be paid a flat fee of $30,000 per month during the term of the Contract.” Pl.’s Mem. at 19; see also id. at 13 (“[T]he Contract between [the parties] provides that Xenophon will be compensated by a monthly payment of $30,000 regardless of the amount of work that is done in any particular month.”). In response, “Jernigan Copeland contends that this provision requires [it] to make a $30,000 advance-fee payment each month, but that it would only be responsible for Xenophon’s billable time spent providing services within the scope of the contract.” Def.’s Opp’n at 1; see also id. at 6-7 (“[Jernigan Copeland] understood the Contract to establish an advance-fee security retainer, whereby Jernigan Copeland would furnish a fixed monthly sum to Xenophon, and Xenophon would record its billable time, furnish these itemized bills to Jernigan [Copeland], and bill directly against the retainer.”).
```

```

Def.’s Opp’n at 17-19. First, Jernigan Copeland notes that section 4.1 “provides that Xenophon will ‘track all hours and supply full detail to the client along with ... monthly invoices.’ ” Id. at 17 (quoting Compl., Ex. 1 (Contract) § 4.1). In addition, Jernigan Copeland notes .that “the Contract authorizes Xenophon to invoice ‘for Services on a monthly.basis, along with [a] six percent professional fee,” id. (quoting Compl., Ex. 1. (Contract) § 5.1(a)), and that Xenophon’s- monthly invoices would include, a “[a] detailed summary of billable time,” Compl., Ex. 1 (Contract) .§ 5.1(a); see also id., Ex. 1 (Contract) § 4.1 (“Xenophon will track all hours and supply full detail to the client along with the[ ] monthly invoices.”). From Jernigan Copeland’s perspective, “Xenophon’s interpretation of the retainer provision as a ‘flat-fee’ monthly $80,000 payment ... would render .the.phrase ‘the Client will be invoiced for Services’ and the phrase ‘a- detailed summary of. billable time’ nullities.” Def.’s Opp’n at 18. (“To assign the meaning of the Contract for which Xenophon argues: that the retainer is money that is owed as, compensation to Xenophon .whether or not the latter performs any work would be to. read this restriction out of the Contract.” And, according- to Jernigan Copeland, under Xenophon’s. interpretation, “there, would -be no reason to distinguish billable time from non-billable .time, nor would there be any reason to. usé the phrase ‘billable time’ at all.”). However, the Court does not find that these two phrases create any ambiguity regarding the word “retainer” as used in section 4.1 of the Contract, nor that they become nullities if the Court accepts Xenophon’s interpretation, of section 4.1 of the Contract as a flat fee monthly retainer. Rather, “the monthly invoices detailing [Xenophon’s] fees and expenses,” in conjunction yith the “detailed summary of billable time,” served as an accounting mechanism that generated an entitlement of actual payment to Xenophon for the work performed. See Compl., Ex. 1 (Contract) § 5.1(a) (“Invoices will be sent on or about the l of each month and payment is due upon receipt. The first invoice of this [Contract will be delivered on or about November 2, 2014 for work performed in October, 2014.”). And, contrary to Jernigan Copeland’s position that these two phrases show that the “ ‘retainer’ was an advance deposit against which fees [would be] drawn,” Def.’s Opp’n' at 17, they indicate that Xenophon would only receive payment for services performed the month immediately after the services were completed and upon Jernigan Copeland’s receipt ' of the invoice, see In re Caesars Entm’t Operating Co., Inc., 661 B.R. 420, 436 (Bankr. N.D. Ill. 2015) (“An advance payment retainer is a payment in exchange for the commitment to provide future legal services.” (emphasis added)). Thus, for thes.e reasons and for the additional reasons set forth below, the Court does not find persuasive Jernigan Copeland’s arguments regarding these two phrases in the Contract.
Contrary to Jernigan Copeland’s position, interpreting the Contract “as a whole [and] giving a reasonable, lawful, and effective meaning to all its terms,” Carlyle Inv. Mgmt. LLC, 131 A.3d at 895 (quoting Debnam, 976 A.2d at 197), the Court construes section 4.1 of the Contract to unambiguously compensate Xenophon with a flat fee of $30,000 plus expenses per month throughout the life of the Contract. As Xenophon notes, the Contract did not include any language indicating that the $30,000 monthly retainer would “be billed against hours and expenses or that any unearned sums will be returned to Jerni-gan Copeland. Indeed, ... it does not contain any requirement of prepayment of fees.” Pl.’s Mem. at 22; see also In re Printing Dimensions, Inc., 153 B.R. 715, 723 (Bankr. D. Md. 1993) (noting that the advance fee retainer arrangement provided that “[a]dditional fees will be charged if the retainer is exhausted,” that fees would be based on “time and results” and that '“[f]inal fees will be based on hourly rates and results” (alterations in original)); In re Dewey & Leboeuf LLP, 493 B.R. 421, 430 (Bankr. S.D.N.Y. 2013) (noting that an “advance payment retainer is not client property!;] the client retains an interest in that portion of the [rjetainer that is not yet earned!;] .,. !and]' at the conclusion of the [contract] ,,. any portion of the advance payment retainer that is not earned” must be. returned to the client). And, because payment for work performed in one month was due the following month upon receipt of the invoice detailing the work performed that preceding month, see Compl., Ex. 1 (Contract) § 5.1(a), the Contract did not call for prepayment or advance payment of fees.
Furthermore, in addition to the two phrases of the Contract relied upon by Jernigan Copeland in support of its position, sections 1.2 and 2.2 of the Contract support the Court’s conclusion that section 4.1 was intended to compensate Xenophon a flat fee of $30,000 per month plus expenses without any limitation based on the hours and services performed during the preceding month. First, section 1.2 provides that “Additional services such as public affairs campaigns required by the client that fall, outside the boundaries of the Scope of Services [jas defined] herein with client approval will be charged at Xenophon’s then-current!] hourly rates.” Compl., Ex. 1 (Contract) § 1.2. Thus, payment for services based on Xenophon’s hourly rates was only for services. performed beyond those identified in the scope of services provision of the Contract as set forth in section 1,1, which, according to section 4.1, are compensated by a $30,000 monthly retainer. See Pl.’s Mem. at 13 (“The only mention of hourly rates in the Contract is in [section] 2.2 ... There is no need to mention hourly rates in a flat fee monthly retainer compensation arrangement since Xenophon’s compensation is not based, on hours worked or hourly rates,”); see also Compl., Ex. 1 (Contract) § 4.1 (noting that Xenophon’s compensation was “[b]ased on the above scope of work” without any indication of an hourly rate). Therefore, accepting Jernigan Copeland’s interpretation that section 4.1 of the Contract provides for an advance feé retainer would amount to “inelud[ing] a provision in the [Contract] that is plainly not there,” which this Court cannot to do. Aziken, 70 A.3d at 220 (quoting Bragdon v. Twenty-Five Twelve Assocs. LP, 856 A.2d 1165, 1170 (D.C. 2004)).
Additionally, section 2.2 states that the “[Contract may be terminated by either party' with [sixty]-days written notice.” Compl., Ex. 1 (Contract) § 2.2. As Xenophon notes, if the Court accepts Jernigan Copeland’s “interpretation of the [Contract as a ‘prepaid’ retainer agreement under which Xenophon is compensated solely on the' basis of hours worked, [section 2.2] would be unnecessary as [Jerni-gan Copeland] could order Xenophon to stop work (and thus stop receiving pay) at any time under [section] 6.1 of the [Contract.” Pl.’s. Reply at 4; see also Compl., Ex. 1 (Contract) § 6.1 (providing that Jer-nigan Copeland “ha[s] the right to modify or stop any schedules or work in progress under this [Contract]; and in such event, Xenophon shall immediately take proper steps to carry out such [instructions”). Consequently, accepting Jernigan Copeland’s position, if it elected to have Xenophon not perform any services, even if only temporarily, Xenophon would “remain[] contractually required to make its staff available as needed to perform the services defined in the Contract” without compensation, Pl.’s Reply at 4, as the Contract would remain viable absent a termination notification as required by section 2.2. Therefore, accepting Jernigan Copeland’s interpretation of section 4.1 as an advance payment retainer would render séction 2.2 meaningless, an outcome inconsistent with the objectives courts in this jurisdiction strive to achieve. See Abdelrhman, 76 A.3d at 891 (“When interpreting a contract, we strive to give reasonable effect' to all of its parts and eschew an interpretation that would render part of it meaningless or incompatible with the contract as a whole.” (citation and internal quotation marks omitted)).
In sum, “the face of [section 4.1] itself ... [and] its plain meaning,” Capital City Mortg. Corp. v. Habana Vill. Art & Folklore, Inc., 747 A.2d 564, 567 (D.C. 2000), coupled with the Court giving “effective meaning to all [the Contract’s] terms,” Carlyle Inv. Mgmt. LLC, 131 A.3d at 895, unambiguously provide Xenophon “with a monthly retainer of $30,000 plus expenses” as a flat fee intended to compensate Xenophon for the services performed under the Contract as defined in section 1.1. Compl., Ex. 1 (Contract) § 4.1.

- **d06** (risk type 1.1, scope `contract`): The word “Services” was disputed as requiring actual logged work after May 1 rather than also encompassing Xenophon’s contractual availability of staff through the Contract’s expiration.
  Opinion lines 37-37:
```
Nonetheless, Jernigan Copeland contends that it is not liable to pay Xenophon’s fees and expenses after May 1, 2015, when it “communicated [to Xenophon the Mississippi State Auditor’s] decision [not to go forward with the tobacco recovery litigation] ... and instructed [Xenophon] to cease work under the Contract.” Def.’s Opp’n at 10; see also id. at 11 (“[Xenophon] had already ceased working under the [Contract, and had already transitioned [its] staff off of the [t]obacco [r]ecovery Mitigation matter.”). However, the clear language of the Contract required a two-month written notice to terminate a party’s obligations under the Contract. See Compl., Ex. 1 (Contract) § 2.2. And, although Jernigan Copeland, as a signatory to the Contract, should have been fully aware of this contractual requirement, Xenophon made efforts to advise Jernigan Copeland to terminate the contract sooner rather than later given the Mississippi State Auditor’s decision, see Pl.’s Mem. at 15 (citing four e-mails Xenophon sent to Jernigan Copeland advising Jernigan Copeland to consider canceling the contract given its financial interest), some of which Jernigan Copeland acknowledged it “overlooked ... [due to] an honest oversight,” Def.’s Opp’n, Ex. 3 (Jerni-gan Aff.) ¶ 30. Moreover, while.
